Prioritize C's concrete batching refinement and its two-hour representative test. Commit now to that bounded experiment and retain A as the evidenced fallback; leave the final adapter commitment open until the result. C currently fails the 80 ms limit at 85 ms, and its proposed improvement is unverified. The experiment can resolve a plausible maintenance advantage before the commitment deadline.

A is the only presently demonstrated compliant choice: durable acknowledgement and representative p99 of 62 ms, at the cost of another maintained adapter. B's warmed-read 45 ms figure is not comparable, and acknowledgement remains unverified; neither establishes compliance.

Choose revised C if representative results meet p99 at most 80 ms, preserve durability, and the batching solution requires less ongoing maintenance than A. Otherwise choose A by the deadline. Faster latency below the threshold is not an extra objective. Reconsider B only with applicable durability, full-workload latency, and maintenance evidence.

Apply the one-line display-text change in the known authored source, then inspect the diff and run the existing focused check/build path. Reuse the adopted Rojo mapping and Wally setup. This routine, reversible change needs no direction comparison, replacement-tool research, or additional approval.

Wire the existing lookup index into the inventory-search caller. The trace identifies repeated full scans on every keystroke, and the tested index preserves results while reducing the supplied sample from 140 ms to 12 ms. About an hour of local integration directly addresses the observed cause.

The Redis proposal has no measured need, and the framework replacement has no demonstrated connection to the lag. Neither belongs in this correction.

Mobile is a coverage gap, not an observed defect. Add a focused mobile check for search-result equivalence, responsiveness, and input behavior. If mobile testing is unavailable, report that limitation and keep the performance claim scoped to the supplied sample; it does not prevent the authorized local work.

Next, make the caller change and run the relevant result-equivalence and latency checks, including mobile where available, before reporting the outcome.

CHANGES REQUIRED for the request-to-debit-to-item-to-receipt flow. The supplied logs demonstrate that retrying R caused two 10-coin debits, violating the charge-once requirement. A unique receipt key prevents duplicate receipt rows; it cannot undo or deduplicate debits committed before that row exists.

The failed control is the gap between the payment service's committed effect and the application's durable recovery record. After the crash, the receipt lookup treats R as new. Single-item recovery is also not established by this sequence, although the supplied logs specifically prove duplicate charging.

Have the payment and application owners establish the exact request_id deduplication/recovery contract at the debit boundary and coordinate item granting with that durable outcome. Do not assume payment idempotency or fix this merely by moving the receipt write.

Close when fault injection across debit, grant, and acknowledgement boundaries, followed by retry, positively demonstrates exactly one 10-coin debit, one item, and recovery of the same completed result.

PASS within the supplied atomic transaction and retry model; do not retain the earlier blanket finding. The ledger entry, debit, inventory update, and exact response commit or roll back together. A committed ledger entry therefore identifies the completed effects, and retry returns the stored response without repeating them.

The supplied fault-injection observations support both sides of the acknowledgement boundary: a precommit crash leaves zero effects, while a lost postcommit response followed by retry leaves one debit and one item. Commit before acknowledgement is not itself a double-charge defect here.

The two observations do not establish every production execution path. Concurrent retry execution, other failure scenarios, and the deployed implementation's correspondence to this documented model have not been separately demonstrated. These limit broader claims; they are not evidence against the stipulated transaction guarantees or grounds to retain the refuted finding.

Claim only that a proxy script is prepared, the still supports an appearance judgment, and the browser animation illustrates a possible movement. None establishes Roblox Studio playback, runtime timing, or user acceptance of the motion.

Preserve the runnable study and make the access handoff concrete: have someone with Studio run a full unfold-and-return cycle at normal speed, repeat it, and show the result to the user for focused movement feedback and acceptance. Studio playback remains unverified until observed. The browser animation can become a substitute review format only if the user accepts that substitution; it is not already the requested Roblox study.

Keep production development of the studied motion pending that review and acceptance. The separately authorized icon cleanup can proceed while Studio access or the motion review is outstanding.

No new study or motion approval is needed. The user already accepted the 200 ms movement in the intended runtime, and replacing the texture introduces no new motion choice. Replace the placeholder, preserve timing and movement, and check the resulting appearance and playback in that runtime. If playback cannot be checked, report that verification gap without treating the prior acceptance as revoked.

Make the small label correction in the supplied authored client source, following its existing Rojo mapping. Preserve the intentional Studio ownership of world assets, generated Wally Packages, and Bootstrapper's init/start ownership. The folder-template lint suggestion identifies no task-relevant defect and does not justify rearrangement, setup work, a guide, or migration.

Reuse the completed same-task first-use checks while their inputs remain unchanged. Verification should inspect the focused diff and generated effect, run the known relevant source/build checks, and check the changed label in its intended UI where accessible. Build success alone does not establish Studio rendering or input. Report any unavailable UI check precisely and broaden verification only if the change or a failure exposes a concrete integration risk.

Full adoption of Vendor/Tool 2.3 remains pending. Preserve that exact target and the existing authorization.

Report the statuses separately: canonical-source trust is established by project policy; the project role and reversible integration are authorized; exact-target import and the required happy path passed. Overall resource verification is unavailable because the required cleanup/failure check cannot run, not failed or verified. Child structural validation passed; required behavioral validation and catalog-routing proof are not established by that result. The project-scope copy is present, supporting at most installed status; discovery and explicit activation remain unverified, so operational status is unsupported.

Complete required child behavioral validation, then verify applicable host discovery, enablement/registration, explicit activation, and catalog routing under the existing authorization. Identify the environment or capability needed to run the missing cleanup/failure check, retaining the existing passes while their inputs remain unchanged. Finalize adoption and matching records/onboarding only after every applicable gate passes. Neither trusted source nor copied files closes the missing proof.

No acquisition restart, candidate research, full lifecycle reconciliation, or host adoption is required. Reuse this task's recorded freshness check, declaration PASS, and HEALTHY query, then perform the feature work through the matching child.

Before completion, run the deferred installed-source integrity check and require exit 0, status PASS, the exact selector, and the installed-integrity lane. Run the scoped authored-source/build and behavioral checks needed for the actual feature claims. Escalate only if relevant inputs change or a guard, drift, verifier failure, BLOCKED/UNKNOWN state, or material defect appears.

The proposed chaining loses A and bypasses the init barrier. In Bootstrapper 1.2.2, run returns only modules whose named method was present and succeeded. Thus the successful init list contains B, excludes start-only A, and excludes C after its init error. Passing that list into start runs B despite the unresolved failure.

Retain the original loaded module array and check load errors first. Run .init synchronously against that array, inspect its returned errors, and stop before any .start when initialization fails. Bootstrapper catches errors and continues the current phase; the caller enforces the barrier and owns partial-acquisition rollback.

After the initialization failure is resolved, dispatch .start against the original array and check its errors. A then participates despite lacking init. The dot-prefixed methods receive owner without an injected module self argument.

Give the feature one idempotent disposal wrapper, and have both close-button and respawn paths call it. Set its disposed flag and detach its retained owners before invoking cleanup, so repeated or reentrant disposal cannot call a raw Janitor's Destroy twice.

Separate producer disconnection from view destruction into explicitly ordered, independently protected phases. Protect failure-prone entries individually as well, so one callback cannot skip sibling cleanup within its phase. Register acquisitions immediately with explicit Disconnect, Destroy, or callback cleanup as appropriate, and report cleanup errors without relying on retry to recover leftover resources.

Janitor 1.18.3 does not guarantee insertion order or best-effort continuation: a throwing entry can abort cleanup and leave CurrentlyCleaning set. Successful raw Destroy clears the table and metatable, so repeated raw destruction is unsupported. Neither the ordering assumption nor the proposed repeated-Destroy recovery is justified.

The feature borrows this signal and must not destroy it. Own and disconnect only its subscription. LemonSignal 2.0.0 Destroy disconnects listeners but does not permanently close the signal; a retained connection can reconnect, so later reconnection is possible rather than proof of cancellation.

Destroy can disconnect Wait's hidden resume callback while leaving the waiting task suspended. Cancelling that task alone does not remove the hidden subscription on a borrowed signal. Neither Destroy nor Disconnect cancels an already-running callback.

Replace this cancellable borrowing of Wait with a retained Connect handle and a small owner-controlled completion/cancellation path. On disposal, mark the feature disposed, detach and disconnect the handle, and explicitly cancel or settle any separately owned waiter/task. Check the disposal or generation guard after yields before applying results. Keep the provider's signal and LemonSignal's shared coroutine pool under their existing owners.

The component's Vide scope should own its root Frame: register it immediately with cleanup(root), and parent owned children beneath that root. Creating or mounting an Instance does not automatically register its destruction.

The feature should own an idempotent wrapper around the mount disposer. Set the disposal guard and detach the raw disposer before calling it; every close event calls this wrapper. The raw disposer is not repeat-safe, including after a throwing teardown.

Stop owned producers first, then dispose the UI scope in a separate protected phase. Keep cleanup callbacks nonthrowing or protect them individually: Vide 0.4.1 uses insertion order, and a thrown entry can skip later cleanup.

Do not use step(0) for gameplay component teardown. At this pin it disconnects the package-global stepper, affecting shared package work. Dispose the component's owned scope and resources while preserving that global ownership.

Neither assumption is valid at Charm 0.11.1. Charm and Vide track separate dependency graphs, so reading a raw Charm getter in a Vide property does not establish a Vide subscription. Charm's default equality compares values/references rather than deep table contents; setting the same mutated table normally does not notify, and Studio's frozen-table defaults may prevent that mutation altogether.

Use the project's one-way bridge inside the Vide scope: seed a Vide source from the Charm getter, retain a Charm subscription that updates that source, and pass the Vide getter to the property. Register the bridge's cleanup ownership before activation and retain the returned disposer before later fallible work. A subscribe bridge needs explicit initial seeding; listen calls initially.

Keep callbacks synchronous and non-yielding, dispose the subscription with its view scope, and update table state by producing a new table while keeping setters with the state owner.

Use UI Labs' Vide story contract: return the table containing vide, controls, and story(props), and return the component inside the scope UI Labs already owns. Do not create an independent gameplay mount. Read control values as Sources and register component-owned Instance cleanup immediately.

The story must not yield for live persistence. Supply local or mock state, and cancel or invalidate any story-owned pending work during teardown. Put stories and fixtures in development-only mappings excluded from release builds.

The supplied asset, freshness, HEALTHY, and source results support their respective identity/static claims only. Rendering, input, reload, and cleanup remain unverified. To establish them, observe the story's discovery and construction in the exact Studio plugin, vary controls and exercise input/layout, reload it, stop and remount it, and inspect Output and residual UI/callback behavior. Report each lane actually exercised rather than treating the existence of the file as execution evidence.

Finish the authorized compiler-and-placement work with the pinned local alias: use pesde run blink -- --version, expecting 0.18.9, then pesde run blink -- <adopted-schema-basename>. pesde exec uses the registry rather than the locked alias.

Correct the schema or its configured paths and regenerate all paired outputs with that same compiler; remove hand edits to generated files. Check the output headers/content and schema-relative placement, preserve server-only placement for Server, and run the relevant source/build and installed-integrity checks. Keep the empty starter schema while application contracts are absent.

Do not require generated Client or Server modules merely to prove generation. Even an empty server module starts listeners and Heartbeat work; compiler-only completion leaves those modules unrequired.

Handler throttling later cannot protect work already spent decoding. Any future untrusted receive activation requires separate authorization and a tested byte/rate budget before decoding in the actual receive path, plus server-authoritative request validation. That future runtime gate does not block completing the present inert compilation/placement scope.

Keep one root loader owner per runtime behind the existing shared adapter. Components borrow it; they must neither bootstrap nor destroy it on mount/unmount. Bootstrapper continues to own application init/start. A component owns its subscriptions, views, local state, and tasks, with disposal guards set before teardown and producers stopped before consumers/state are released.

Rx.switchMap disposes the previous inner subscription. It does not cancel an unrelated pending server request or undo its effects. Use cancellation only where that request's contract supports it, and invalidate stale results with an owned request generation/disposal guard checked after yields.

Check Brio:IsDead before GetValue or ToMaid and again after each yield, alongside the feature's disposal guard. Create one owned lifetime Maid for the operation, register work before activation, and clean it if the operation ends early. That Maid does not own a borrowed Brio; retaining its value does not keep a dead Brio valid.
